Fascinating little game with a very interesting RPG system, which is based on resource management and probability.

Building your character feels challenging but rewarding, especially since it's very difficult to get new permanent upgrades as they're sparse and depend on being lucky most of the times.
The combat is surprisingly deeper than one could think at the start, with talking and trading being interactions that you'll unlock on the later stages of a run, which expand what you can do by a lot.

The story is extremely abstract, for the couple of runs I did I'm only vaguely understanding what's happening, but it's part of the course with this game, so I won't judge it right now. Instead I want to gush for a second on how cool and atmospheric the whole thing looks, it's probably one of its stronger traits!

The price is also very affordable, which is always welcome, I'd recommend it even without it being on sale honestly.

Tried it without really knowing anything about it. The game opens with a poorly written dialogue that may put some off. After this, I've become a little hooked and want to play again - I had only wanted to play for 5minutes before sleeping but played 2 'playthroughs'. 

There's a brooding, dreamlike, abstract yet malevolent atmosphere akin to Silent Hill. Looking beyond the basic visuals, the game design is actually excellent with meaningful choices presented to the player constantly.

Its a fun rogue-like. The dialogue is mostly tortured poet jabber, but sometimes hides clues to solving puzzles. Runs largely rely on RNG, but generally, you're trying to either buff your gun, your knife, or (if you're lucky) you can go the smoker route and stack item damage on cigarettes to smoke bosses in a single turn. Its more of a resource management game than combat game as each encounter has some kind of "cost" - either HP or Items - and you have to balance your expenses to ensure you survive. You've got shards as an additional currency for trades with either shops or enemies themselves during the third round. The final round is brutal as its 4 (multi-round) bosses back to back and they will overwhelm you if you don't have enough items or damage output. 

Is it deep? No, but its also $7 (less on sale), and for a $7 game its good.

I found NO-SKIN by chance, thanks to watching Markiplier and seeing him play one of the early beta versions of the game. It became immediately clear that NO-SKIN had tons of potential, a strong art direction and aesthetic, and a story it was passionate about telling. And the more I played, the more the betas progressed, the more apparent it became that this was bound to become my favorite roguelike.
NO-SKIN is characterized by tantalizing mysteries, a unique and strong aesthetic, and a chilling horror tone. Every battle feels like a grungy fight where you exchange blows and you cannot escape unscathed. The tension is high no matter how strong you get. Not only is that challenge already addictive, but the mystery is even more so.
The game's story strikes the same kind of balance the first Five Nights at Freddy's did. There's this implicit promise that nothing in the game is added unintentionally, and that if you dig deep enough you'll find answers. I recall playing the beta, seeing the true Luna speak in garbled text, and then freaking out with a friend when we realized you could use the translator as a Rosetta stone to translate her words. Enemies occasionally offer you hints on unique interactions and lore reveals. And everything makes the larger picture more tragic, yet you can't stop looking, like a car crash in slow motion.
What I desire more than anything would be a demake or port of this game to handhelds. Playing this game on my Deck is so immensely satisfying and feels so right, but the Deck proves to be a bit large and excessive to run a game of this scale. I beg of you, No-eyesoft, please find a way to release the game on mobile, or demake it for the gameboy advance, Nintendo DS or PS Vita. Or if you are a fan, please take up the challenge yourself. It's the only thing that could make me love this game more than I already do.

You see, the game's combat, while really basic in isolation, is designed to carry on your performance through the entire run. That is, your decisions in each individual battle will influence your chance to win this particular run. 

Even more so, choosing who to fight is an important decision - since each enemy always drops the same items (and items are very, very important, very very and much much… imperch), you want a particular enemy at a specific turn to get through a boss fight later.

The lack of on-demand healing is another major consideration that influences your approach to even the simplest enemies. You can't really just spam with your knife attack.

But there's more! Permadeath games have an inherent form of metaprogression called "player's knowledge" - which is so often gets forgotten by roguelite developers who are too busy implementing mechanical forms of a metaprogression. NO-SKIN has secret interactions both with enemies and with events that can be very helpful later on.

All in all, NO-SKIN is a very fun roguelite with cool and unique vibe, fast and strategical gameplay, and some kinda story too!

The game just exudes cool. It's such a simple idea executed to perfection. a really creepy, unsettling roguelike that feels punishing but not unapproachable to play. I have a pretty weak heart when it comes to horror stuff but this game doesn't have any jumpscares for the most part (a couple of unexpected noises is all I can remember). the horror is mostly in the situation, imagery and subtext. speaking of which, there's a lot of themes of suicide and self-harm in particular in the game so if you're particularly sensitive to that be careful.

the combat system is very simple to understand but you can't really 'master' it insofar as repeated battles will inevitably wear you down, exhausting either your health or your items. the metaprogression doesn't really help in this regard either, since most of it is just extra stuff you can encounter rather than upgrades to your character, though some of the unlockable shop items are undeniably helpful.

there are no safe plays in this game. even in navigation, each location has a range of possible encounters, with at least one of which always being a fight. even something so simple as accessing a merchant comes with the risk of encountering something that wants you dead instead. in theory it's an incredibly RNG based game in that respect, it certainly felt that way for my first hour or so, but you can still make decisions to help even the odds. if you're low on health in chapter 1, going to the bathroom is usually a good option. even if you don't get one of the events that just heal you, the fights there reward you with a healing item anyway.

the game balances its own rng a little in that way. generally speaking whatever you might've gotten for free you'll still get for winning the fight in the same room. the exceptions to this rule tend to be the more risk-reward rooms. do you risk fighting an unkillable enemy, wasting a time slot and potentially health and/or items while running away, to potentially get a greater boon? (tip: the answer is often yes)
I'm pretty confident that the game is supposed to feel punishing to play (for narrative purposes) but it still does its part to feel like a game where you have agency rather than just a pain simulator.

as for the narrative... it's hard to tell. there's a lot of thematic and unsettling things going on as the protagonist seemingly loses all grasp on reality, and most of the enemies are increasingly distorted versions of your friends from the intro cutscene. there isn't a lot of talking or explaining, though. you do eventually remember how to talk later in the game but none of the enemies are particularly willing to explain the situation to you, mostly just threatening or insulting you. or pleading for help.
the game does eventually start pulling some threads together (which I won't say here) but for the most part it just leaves you to make your own interpretations on what the hell is going on and how much of what you're seeing is actually real.
I quite liked trying to piece together themes in this way but I can understand if other people find it frustrating or lacking in substance.

I should mention also that the game does have a scaling difficulty system (faith level, analogous to ascension in slay the spire etc.) and there is one level below the default buyable cheap from the metaprogression shop. I haven't actually played with this reduced difficulty mode so I can't say how much difference it makes but I assume it would make for an easier path to explore the game's content. another little tip from me if you're struggling is that enemy move patterns [spoiler]aren't random. they follow the same sequence each time you fight them.[/spoiler]

This game is not a turn-based RPG, though it may at first seem so. This game is a puzzle/mystery game that uses RPG mechanics to pace the story, as well incentivize the player to learn more about the world NO-SKIN presents the player. I will go deeper, and while I won't give spoilers, just in case you want to experience the game COMPLETELY BLIND, I suggest playing the demo.

I played the game when it was at it's demo stage, and I can say with confidence the game keeps that EXACT same style and mood, and expands on mechanics and goals. If you like the demo, you'll love the full release.

When I say that NO-SKIN is not a "turn-based RPG", I mean it in the same way that a sculpture made out of different colored M&Ms isn't "food". As is acknowledged in a secret room of the game, the combat loop can get extremely repetitive and easily bore you over longer play sessions.

This is why your goal when playing NO-SKIN should be to unpack the mystery of what is going on, and to solve small puzzles throughout the game to make your character stronger through the knowledge you gain. Most of the power you gain in NO-SKIN doesn't come from items or upgrades, but from understanding what each room offers you, and discovering the hidden interactions that can make you significantly stronger than any item alone could.

The reason I stress that this game should be played spoiler-free, is that the game, while subtle about its mysteries, WANTS you to solve them and beat the game. Now what do I mean by this? 

Take a game like "Nix Umbra", there are many hidden mechanics in that game, but they are in no way shape or form player friendly to discover. I would argue it is completely impossible to learn even a handleful of secrets and mechanics by oneself, unless you plan on dedicating dozens of ours in that game. Nix Umbra is flawed in that despite only having maybe a dozen or so secrets, a player cannot be expected to find many of them on their own, so they are forced to just google everything, removing all mystery and suspense. A small puzzle is no fun if the player cannot be expected to solve it without cheating.

A game like "TUNIC" is the exact opposite. The game has many secrets that are designed to be discovered by the player that puts in a reasonable amount of work. But ON TOP OF THAT, there are also many MASSIVE secrets that require a community-wide goose hunt to fully uncover, making the best out of both worlds, as even if the small secrets are mostly spoiled for yourself, it can still be fascinating to learn about the super hidden secrets in the game. Bigger puzzles can be fun through the cooperation a community needs to solve them, though the puzzle must be big to make this happen.

NO-SKIN falls in between these two categories, as while I don't believe there exists a giant community-wide secret in the game (though I may be wrong the game was released like 2 days ago), there are plenty of smaller secrets that the player is expected to solve throughout the game. In simple terms, a puzzle game is no fun if you already know the solution, and the same applies here. The puzzles in this game are perfectly balanced as far as I can tell, so avoid as much spoilers as you can and the "eureka!" moments you will get will feel absolutely amazing.

If you are wondering about flaws in this game, yes they exist, but overall can be overlooked. Some of the flaws I hope to be patched are as follows:
-Just as is said in one of the secret rooms, the 4th wall breaks feel like they're just breaking something else. The issue is that they occur far too often. I think the 4th wall breaks should occur once every 5-10 play-through's, and add an upgrade in the permanent shop to make them happen every single run when you've already beaten the game.
-The difficulty of the game is far too easy, even at higher faith levels. I am unsure what the maximum faith level is, but I would recommend making the difficult increase ramp up faster, as I felt that faith level 4 was about as difficult as faith level 2 should have been. Also, maybe incentivize players to play at higher faith levels by giving more Lunar fragments at higher faith levels, and half as many at faith 0.
-Some of the events or texts in the game come off as either edgy in a cringe way, childish or immature. This isn't something that ruins the game by any means, it just pulled me out of the game personally, and if No-eye-soft believes it is truly important for the story they are trying to tell, I will overlook those aspects. One of the lines that come to mind is the line before the final phase of the NO-SKIN-MAN when you do not have the skin. When you are called a "female-dog" (to follow steam's guidelines) it comes off as pretty odd. ONCE AGAIN i'm not a sensitive person by any means, its just that weird character moments such as that pull me out of the experience.

To recap, this is a great game, but be sure that you are buying this game for the mystery and puzzles, NOT for the RPG combat aspect. The game isn't perfect by any means, but it's unique and interesting enough in its excecution to warrent a playthrough by those who love a good puzzle or mystery.

No-skin is a simple, yet haunting RPG Roguelite Horror that increasingly gets more challenging and sometimes feel like a puzzle to be solved rather than a wall to smash through.

Despite its straightforward presentation and limited mechanics, the game's depth feels like an abyss the more you let the disturbing atmosphere sinks in, like an eldritch horror's dream.

[h1]In Short[/h1]
The game is relatively simple, it's a turn-based RPG where you have to plan your move, attack the enemies, use items, run away or even some odder mechanics like talking and trading with them. Each enemy will respond differently based on what you do, there are more hidden interactions that are hinted upon as well.

Using your items and taking actions wisely is the key to survival and fishing a run. Finishing a run isn't the end, each run you will not only unlock something else you can use, but you will slowly unravel what is happening. Whether you can unravel the entire story or not... I don't know, I've not gotten too far.

But so far, the atmosphere of the game is absolutely impeccable, turn off the lights, put on your headphones, and let the abyss stares. 

As a sidenote, personally I wouldn't be playing the game constantly to completion, take breaks, then get back to it, don't overwhelm yourself with the game, let it slowly guides you to its world. 

[h1]Recommendation[/h1]
Personally, a total recommendation, this game contains an amazing creepy atmosphere and a puzzle-like combat mechanics that push you to feel the horror in your heart, not in your face.

Initially, you may think the game isn't that hard, but the more you play, the more difficult it gets. Though, the game isn't about making sure you will lose, it's about making you think about assembling the puzzle pieces. As for why, I guess you'll just have to figure it out yourself.

[h1]Extra thoughts[/h1]
[b]Mechanically[/b], the game's is straight forward, you attack or defend consuming a turn, while using items, talking or trading don't consume a turn. However, there is no free lunch, every action has a consequence that you'll have to calculate. While not encountering enemy, you'll get a randomly generated set of location to move to, with each location has a chance of triggering different events, so picking the right course of events to let you succeed in a run is absolutely essential. And with each run, the amount of locations may increase, giving you both more choices to make and risks to take.

The battle encounters are structured like puzzles, not only there are sometimes hidden mechanics for an enemy, but they have their own patterns of attacks and tells, you'll have to adapt your strategy because you can't just out-level your enemies like traditional RPG games, this is a roguelite! While there are permanent upgrades you can make between runs... don't count on them to make you overpowered, you're always on the verge of annhilation in this game.

[b]Thematically[/b], the game doesn't tell you much, is anything real? Is everything a delusion? Or both? Who knows, the game's simplistic designs are deceptive, in those darkness and blank space, it gives way to imaginations, if you're the type of gamer who let the atmosphere, the world sink into your head, you'll find horrors lurking around the darkness, the unknowns bring about the greatest amount of uneasiness.

[b]Sound designs[/b], are fantastic, special mention, despite there being no voicework in the game, the music and sounds in the game will constantly make you feel uneasy, casting a fog over your whole experience. Please don't play the game on mute, it's like disabling the fog in Silent Hills! Instead, let the game's sounds lead you into its world and creeps into your mind.

I'm giving this a slight recommend. I think for the price there's some interesting stuff here, but overall it falls flat and I have significant criticisms with the game as a whole.

As the game shows, this is essentially a turn-based horror roguelite experience. The core gameplay and the one you'll spend the most time in is the No-Skin mode with the goal of getting to 100% (at first). Essentially though, the game is all about managing resources. Understanding which rooms to go for if you need life/ammo/instant damage, fishing for upgrades/shops and fighting enemies with minimal resource loss. For me at least this system was fairly simple (having beaten the game past Faith 4 + extra bosses) and for the most part it wasn't very difficult. Which is perfectly fine, but one of the core problems the game has is tedium. There are a lot of repeated text boxes, enemies have a fairly low amount of dialog, and getting into the later half of the game where you need to optimize trades for items/health etc exacerbates the problem. For the most part bosses are knowledge checks, if you didn't get to a boss with specific resources or items you're likely to lose.

Which brings me to the second critique: There's a fairly low amount of variety. Enemies tend to all behave very similarly, there's a small pool of upgrades both from the shop(s) and from the meta progression. It means whatever character you play will tend to always play the same.

Gameplay-aside, the story and characters is probably the bit I'm most lukewarm on. You're introduced to the same characters in different contexts (battle, dream diary) but for the most part there really isn't much there. You get brief glimpses into a characters personality, but none of it really comes together in a way that is coherent. In many aspects it feels like the game is both doing too much and too little, the parts where the game tries to break the mold are interesting but it does so with such frequency that it reduces the novelty.

The artwork is generally really good though along with the ambiance, but that's unfortunately not enough to really carry forward gameplay that is just sort of there and a story that can't decide what it's actually trying to do. I think it's still a unique enough title that's worth a look, but ultimately I'd consider the game to be a resounding 'Okay'.

[h2]Some Chafing[/h2]

This is going to be one of those "It's good, but" reviews.

Imagine a body of living, breathing meat. Now picture a wrapping of skin for it that doesn't quite fit right. With me? Okay, so the meat is the guts of a classic roguelike experience and the skin in this case is the horror atmosphere. I'm going somewhere with this.

At first, the two move as one. You select a new room, see a surreal horror accompanied by an eerie soundtrack, and you're on edge. The meat twitches. The skin twitches with it. Grotesque harmony.

Over time however, that ill fitting causes the meat to unsync with the skin. Roguelikes adore repetition, and repetition abhors horror. Revisiting the same rooms, encountering the same nasties with the same spooky soundtrack ceases to terrify, nopeify, or even reach significant levels of perturbification. Once you clear the game, then it's time to run it again on Prestige 1. Then Prestige 2. Then again. Again. again. A fresh sting here and there does help, but eventually that skin is worn down to callouses through friction with the meat, leaving the player feeling numb.

For the price, it's value enough for those first few runs. If you're looking for games that better blend a horror & rogue-like experiences however, here's some I'd consider ahead of this title.

[b]World of Horror[/b] 
Why it works better? [i]Plenty:[/i] There's just more of this game then No-Skin. It will hold your attention longer before you're familiar with its awfulness, although with a price point to match.

[b]Inscryption:[/b] 
Why it works better? [i]Variety:[/i] The gameplay experience and atmosphere are prone to twists and turns, keeping you on edge. It is less of a strict horror experience, so those seeking spooks solely might not be sated.

[b]Fear and Hunger / Terminus:[/b] 
Why it works better? [i]Agony:[/i] These games hurt you through vicious encounters and a startling degree of depth, drawing you deeper into its foul pits, only to snuff you out from a single misstep, daring you to try again from the top. You cannot help but feel tense with every moment you spend in these games, although they both sabotage that tension at times with juvenile body horror (Terminus is better about it).

If you've played and vibed with the above, No-Skin will feel right at horrid home. Just don't wear out your welcome.

When you win battles, you earn two types of currency. Lunar Fragments are used for meta-progression, unlocking upgrades and new options between runs, which you can enable or disable. Crimson Fragments are spent during the run itself: on buying items and, if needed, to bribe enemies out of kicking your ass.

The game is RNG-based, so you might love it… or hate it XD

This game has a lot going for it: secrets to uncover, a story that takes multiple runs to piece together, and some surprisingly tough encounters. Be warned though—progress usually means replaying, and a lot of the good stuff is locked behind puzzles or hidden paths. Don’t expect many guides either, so most of the discovery is on you.

Bosses will crush you if you don’t learn their mechanics, and the Dream Diary (if you unlock it) houses some of the hardest fights. You’ll die a lot, but the game does give you tools—extra items, new shops, and mechanics that open up as you figure things out. Run times vary—quick ones can be 15–45 minutes, while deeper runs can stretch well past 2 hours, especially if you’re solving puzzles or hitting new bosses for the first time.

[quote]"You're dead. Your friends are dead. Your family is dead. Your ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ pets are being skinned alive. Your mom's a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ♥♥♥♥♥. You suck at life. The whole world hates you. You're going to Hell. Live with it. Game Over."[/quote]
NO-SKIN is a psychotic urban punk fairytale that plays like World of Horror if it was made by Daniel Mullins high off the Draft of Darkness' kitchen sink residue. I'm not flaunting the verbiage here, it's exactly as bizarre as it sounds. Be wary that this game bathes in gore and self-harm. If you aren't ready, you might find it getting under your skin upsetting. Now, it all begins with a group of friends discussing relatable topics like long shifts and lousy management. The friendliness ends soon after as the world goes dark. Your name is Noire and you drank too much, now you see a flayed man standing in the dark hallway on stubs for legs. He asks you where his skin is and demands it back. "Until you do, I will show you things as they really are." This is not a gift. Your apartment becomes a death trap, but don't despair. The Moon Goddess shall lend you a hand by bestowing her blessings and bringing you back to life. It's a roguelite, after all. The game immediately tells you that each action ends your turn except for items in your bag, which you can use to your heart's content, stacking up buffs. It does so to emphasise that consumables can do just about anything, so be resourceful, hoard, watch your only stat - hp. Weapons have 2 stats: damage and accuracy. By default, a knife is weak, yet a gun needs ammo. Both can be modified in unconventional ways.

Having all that resource management in mind, you pick between rooms to enter. Each presents you with a list of events that could happen, their probabilities on display. Agency is king, make it count. On entering a room, you roll for an event and make even more choices. Partake in turned-based JRPG-like combat with clearly stated intents, kill to loot items as well as two types of currency that allows you to buy items from frogs and fish or recall memories for meta-progression upon death. When you don't fight, you solve surreal conundrums. Help the hanged man at the expense of some health? Play Russian roulette with a skeleton? You could talk to monsters, propose a trade, even hire one like it's Megami Tensei! Soon, you'll find out the intricacies of your bitter relations with your condemnatory frenemies. Nothing is as simple as it seems, there's a subtle questing system in place. But let's not dwell on something you'd rather discover for yourself. Action by action, you obtain a percentage of finding the skin, your Golden Fleece and a carrot on a stick. No-skin Man's curse intensifies as you progress no matter what you do, making your enemies stronger and your memories more vivid. Thus, you unlock more and more rooms to visit, muster an arsenal of items and perks, then pass thresholds, going deeper to face nasty bosses who sometimes cheat.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3464603841
Are you tripping? Is it a prank or a nightmarish delusion that forces you to murder your friends for real? Their caustic visages deteriorate alongside your glitching world. You constantly learn about them and the game, which never ceased to entice me with its raw emotion. Is it a story about human bonds? Penitence? A hard life? The throughline stitching its threads together is elusive. I won't tell you what's going on since the intrigue stemming from a simple premise is the bait. Besides, it would merely be my interpretation, not something certain. What I can tell is that this isn't a disposable kind of deal. It's too mental to get stale ahead of time. You'll unlock difficulties, characters with different agendas, and side-puzzles of the Dream Diary, expanding your knowledge and meta. When you think you broke the code, the labyrinth of suffering keeps growing with each beating like a bruise. At that, the game can be grindy and could use a fast-forward button for the repeated text. But it's a fun affair regardless. With clever mechanics to wrap your head around while taking wrapper after wrapper off this sour candy. It's cruelly hard, too, but offers an easy mode. Almost no strings attached. So, be not afraid, NO-SKIN was designed to appeal to a wider audience without losing its punk edge. This game earns its grit. First, it catches your eye, then slowly burrows into your brain.

Gameplaywise the game is quite simple and somewhat in roguelike manner: 3 acts, 3 bosses, plus final boss gauntlet, 50ish rooms in between. Choose between 3 rooms and get your percentage what happens. Specific combat encounters guarantee a specific item. You get your melee attack, your ammo reliant range option, block, escape... item-usage does not require a turn and the game revolves a lot around this, resourcefulness.; while there is a lot of chance involved, every percentage lies in front of you, so you get some agency in the RNG-jungle. But hey, it is still RNG - gotta love it or hate it.
Later on you even get a "Talk" and "Trade", these are also quite unique.

Storywise I have absolutely no idea what is going on; the cast of all those edgegirls as NPCs and playercharacters didn't really pick me up, they are quite literally faceless. But apart from the dark moody broody teenage angst tropiness it embodies, the whole ordeal still has a fascinating dreamlike shape and some genuinely off vibes [spoiler] for unlocking the true ending you literally have to go out of bounds and face the dev as a boss, this was - while not entirely new - quite nice. Also liked that in the fight against the false god you see idols of faith, wealth and family, before his true face literally becomes de Goyas Saturn devouring his son, very well played touch! No-Skin is a rogue-like game where each turn you get three random room choices to make. In these rooms you either get to fight monsters, find items, or engage with weird oddities. The goal of the game is to find the Skin of a monster called the No-Skin Man, which is a convoluted mess to obtain. This game has a deep rabbit hole of lore and secrets to discover, some may play for 5 hours and be satisfied, others may play for 15 hours and keep discovering new little pieces of lore.

+ The art style of the game is highly original. The enemies are interesting and disturbing.
+ The music in the game is hauntingly beautiful, in a Silent Hill / Liminal space kind of way.
+ The dialog is always engaging, very humorous at times.
+ A massive amount of secrets to dig up: hidden mini-games, hidden characters, hidden enemies, hidden gameplay elements to unlock. 
+ Dreary, dreadful atmosphere that never lets up.

+/- On the surface the gameplay seems simple at first glance, however as you play more you will discover the gameplay is actually very deep and engrossing after you discover all the intricacies.
+/- There is a long and deep story here to dig up after playing for 10+ hours, but it is also a convoluted mess. In the end it's not really understandable or worth the effort of what the game puts you through to get it.

- There will be times you will play for hours, and make zero progress. This gets frustrating and tiresome.

Individual mileage will vary. For me, at 6 hours in, after unlocking all the perks, with 2 hours of trying to defeat the last secret boss to get the game's one achievement, my patience flew out the window and I'm moving on.
Had some fun while it lasted!

Overall: 6.5/10

Buy it. Don't read the rest of this review. Don't look at the preview images. Just play it blind. This game is fantastic. One of a kind experience.

Now, for the rest of the review: Where do I even begin? despite the game being a FRACTION of a gigabyte in size, there is SO MUCH TO DO. I can tell I'm not even close to being done with it after 4 hours. However I can already tell how special this game truly is.

The atmosphere is extremely odd and unnerving. The pixel art and the music & ambient droning all do a really good job giving this game a very unique feeling. Pair that with the enigmatic and bizarre writing and very obfuscated and non linear story being told and it truly becomes special.

The soundtrack is great and extremely memorable. The music is extremely varied while still making sure to keep within the very specific feel the game is going for and it ALL works really well.

The gameplay has a lot of variance and depth. the game CAN be a *little* punishing with it's rng sometimes, but outside of that minor nitpick the game is fluid, easy to pick up, but has TONS of room for knowledge checking that let you feel INCREDIBLY smart as you do more runs.

The story is an interesting one. Like I said I think I am still VERY early on in figuring anything out, and even then the way everything is told is so off-kilter and jarring that I can't say there will ever be a concrete plot for me to tie a neat little bow on at the end. But despite not having seen much and figured out even less, the game still OOZES emotion. The bleak, claustrophobic atmosphere just dampens your mood in such a specific way. Playing the game I have such a swirl of sadness and unease that clashes so harshly with the feeling of triumph as you progress through the game that I cannot help but remember every step forward I make. 

This game is surely creeping up my top games of the year. Won't likely be number 1, but I can HANDILY see a top 5 spot for me when the year closes out.

Ah No-Skin, I remember playing the demo. It hooked me, grabbed my by my hair and pulled me into this horrific nonsensical world, where nothing is as it truly is.

Whats not to like? A charming pixelated art style with spooky horror elements. A cast of fun and interesting characters. All tied together with simple, but fun game play and easy to learn mechanics.

I want to talk about the characters first because, its funny, and I really do enjoy them. You have, a guy with no skin. His son, who also has no skin and a timidness not expected. An attractive fish with long gills, sentences that leave you baffled, and shocking good deals. A Goddess, who drafts you to realize Her will. Frogs, who sell you wares from the trash and say things like, "Frogs, Frogs, we are Frogs". Whats not to love. The game also has multiple playable characters, each with their own gimmicks, albeit some better than others.
-
Take Luna for example... *cough* Best Girl *cough cough* ... She starts with 3 base damage, a lot, but suffers from terrible accuracy. This can easily be paired with another item from the Frogs and she easily becomes significantly stronger. Not only that but that isin't even her gimmick, thats just how great she is. But enough fawning, lets move on.

The art style is incredible unique, mainly using pixel art. With the game being horror it uses that to create these grotesque, characters and places, that really put you in this world that is not your own. There is explicit content, in the manner of blood, deformations, drinking, drugs, and nudity. Pray to the Goddess your Mom doesn't walk in when your fighting 'The Competition'.

With turn based combat, the game play is incredibly easy to learn, you stab, you shoot, you pray, and you run, almost everything else is a free action. Stabbing and shooting are your main methods of dealing damage, although your run could result in you killing things with second hand smoke from cigarettes. Praying is how you defend, it sets the damage you take that turn to 1. This is mainly used for when enemies take the turn before to prepare to unleash a devastating attack, but once again, it could have other uses depending on your run. Running away is just that, some enemies can't die without special means, that you often don't have. So you run, which can fail, which will result in the enemy taking its turn, and an increase in your escape chance. You also have an inventory, but that one is extremely flexible because, for most of the game, you can use as many items as you want without using your turn.

No-Skin is a great game, and I 100% recommend it, and for $6 it's not unbearable expensive, and it definitely has enough content to make it worth it. It does get difficult at times, but that just makes you feel that much better when you finally do finish that goal.
-
I'm not going to lie though, it does get difficult, an example is the Trish diary, a puzzle you get for completing the game multiple times. The Trish diary was insanely difficult, I probably sunk 2 hour in it until I finally beat it. Before beating it though, I had a run go to its boss, proceed to knock it down to one health, miss once, and die. It was a play perfectly, get killed because you missed once challenge. But you know whats even better than a challege?
-
THE DEV NERFED IT! No-Eye Soft listens to the players, and updates the game accordingly, which means No-Skin has a lot of room to grow from where it is now, with player support. Which is extremely important for any game.

There is a man with no skin standing in the hallway. You have to find it's skin.
That is all the introduction you get before being thrusted into the world of No-Skin. As a game, it looks unfair: enemies hit pretty hard and, chances are, you'll die pretty quickly. That's to be expected from a turn based roguelike tho, part of what made this game fun are the small realizations that there are ways to beat the creatures you encounter, things like noticing that their attack patterns are never random, knowing what rewards they give and what resources you should have before facing them, for someone like me figuring out those strategies are the fun part of this genre. That's not what made this game *special* tho. It made it fun, sure, but what made it *special* are the things it *hides* from you, and all the secrets you can uncover. 
This game is a *lot* more complex than what the main campaign would make you believe, and that's because the game goes out of its way to hide these from you. The best example I can share without taking away too much of the joy of finding those things on your own is that very scene at the end of every encounter showing you your progress. From that bar, which shows how close you are to finding the skin, implies that each run is a straight line, you start here and progress there. When you see that, you don't expect there to be different routes you can take, or even that you can go backwards. But there are, and you can, and the things you encounter outside of the boundaries of the world itself made this game great for me. And I dare not speak much of it, because there's some things in this game that are wonderful to experience yourself.
The story itself is nothing special, it's baby's first toxic yuri, but the way its told makes it a lot stronger for me. While in most cases a simple story told in a complicated way would take away from my enjoyment of a game, this is a rare case where I believe that it is done well. I will elaborate on that a bit more in a moment, but it's one of those cases where at the end I had to ask myself what really happened and what did not, the same kind of question I had at the end of games like Katana Zero and the entire reason why The Shining stayed on my mind despite watching it so many years ago. And to be clear, that question really only works if the story doesn't give a straight answear, it only works if I have to ponder it for much longer than the time I actually spent on the media itself. And the Vibes? God, the Vibes are *spot on*.
But that's not really the horror of no-skin, is it? No, the horror of this game is much more insidious, built into the story itself. The horror that has actually gotten to me in this game is the realization that you yourself are not a good person. It's the realization that you're really only hurting the people you care, that the people around you are just enabling your own toxic traits and you enabling theirs. The realization that everyone is miserable, and your very fault in it. As someone who has been through that myself, that kinda hits hard, and I found it pretty damn well written. The characters feel surprisingly realistic for something written by a dev that, as far as I can find, has no experience writing this kind of story. Bravo to the dev to be honest.
Granted, it's not without criticism. My main issue with the game is the complete and utter lack of build variety. Almost none of the item drops and upgrades you can get are random, the exceptions being the crimson dancers and the encounters you get. While I understand the importance of having guaranteed upgrades in a game like this (I agree that having some way of skipping progress percentage in the final floor is important), having *all* of them be guaranteed just makes every run feel the same. It's a very homogeneous kind of roguelike, where although the builds you *always* (emphasis on always) end up with have some minor variations, they all play and feel the exact same. That I think is the worst aspect of this game. (I've seen some people complain that the game is too rng reliant, which really makes me wonder if we played the same game cuz frankly once you get it you realize how little rng there actually is)
I also don't like that the game just straight up tells you what to do next after you beat the final boss. Feels like handholding, the average player *can* figure that out and it was already the thing I was planning on trying out while facing the boss. Kind of a minor nitpick but, y'know, I do think the game would be better without it. Regardless, absolute fire game, absolute recommend if you're into that kinda thing (Which I am).

One of the more interesting Gamemaker rougelikes in recent memory. This game does three things really well: pretentious indie vibes, run optimisation, and cool secrets It doesn't really do anything else, but that was no issue for me because I love all three of these things.

The premise of the game is that you are a girl with a group of friends (?) who is tripping really hard and the lines between reality and nightmarish revelations of the world are blurring. You progress the main story by winning multiple runs and completing several character-specific puzzles until you reach the true ending. The narrative of the game is hard to follow on purpose, but you don't need to know what's happening to enjoy the vibes. Finding an item or enemy and thinking "oh cool, this thing looks like something from the protagonist's life but it's all messed up!!" was the main source of interest for me. Maybe I'm sleeping on the deep themes of this game, but honestly the vibes alone kept me satiated and I was never bored or annoyed at my own confusion. I thought the ending was quite cool and it made more sense than I expected it to.

Gameplay-wise, it's a pretty straightforward turn-based dungeon crawler. You choose one of three offered events and roll the dice regarding the outcomes and what enemies you'll have to fight. Very luck-dependent, but also surprisingly consistent and transparent. The odds of every single dice roll in the game are shown to you before the rolls are made, which gives you a lot of control regarding what choices you'll make. It's hard to feel cheated by bad luck if you've been warned about it. 

The run optimisation comes in the fact that although events are randomly selected for you, the actual contents are entirely predetermined. Enemies will (barring the special secret ones) follow the same patterns, appear in the same rooms, offer the same trades, etc. Eventually, you will learn how to use this information to completely annihilate every single run. To mitigate how easy the game becomes once you've "solved" it, there are some additional difficulty modes you can unlock. They don't offer any real rewards for completing but I think they're essential to have fun once you can do normal runs on autopilot. I think I got up to Faith 6 before I got the true ending, and even then I wasn't having much trouble.

The secrets of this game are really fun and weird. The most random actions you may do on a whim can lead to unexpected discoveries. My favourites were discovering what trades certain enemies had were overpowered and abusable, as well as figuring out how to [spoiler]recruit[/spoiler] certain enemies. I think the hypest moment for me was unlocking a character that can progress [spoiler]backwards[/spoiler]. After getting over how neat of an idea that was, it dawned on me that I could use all my game knowledge to make the most broken run possible. Super, super neat!

I don't really have many negative things to say. I don't think the game is infinitely replayable, and I don't have any interest in revisiting it after getting the true ending. But reaching that ending was really fun and worth the money. One thing that ticked me off was a bit in a puzzle where [spoiler]a character reads out a hypothetical negative review for this game, focusing on specific shortcomings. I don't like it when games do this. Have some confidence in this cool thing you've birthed, you've earned it![/spoiler]

Uhhh tl;dr it's a Gamemaker turn-based rougelike that excels at pretentious indie vibes, run optimisation, and cool secrets. Not for everyone, but it was for me :-)

[h1] If I did not have Expedition 33 as my personal GOTY, this would be it. [/h1]

I had bought this game on a whim, I don't remember exactly when. I just knew that this looked like something I would enjoy, and I think it came recommended from a tweet from the guy who made the game, IMSCARED (either they retweeted a post or mentioned it directly, I do not know for certain, I just know that it came from somewhere around there). It was only a couple of dollars, so even if I didn't like it, I was not incentivized to go return it because I was certain I could find something that I liked about it beyond the trailer and store images and support the effort that was put into this work.

There it sat in my library for a long while, always on that mental backlog, and thinking "I should get to that." The icon and name always stood out against everything else in my library, so it managed to eventually escape the backlog and catch my attention again after practically marathoning Final Fantasy XVI. I needed something small, something digestible, but something that was completely and exclusively up my alley.

I didn't think it would actually suck me in as much as it did. I just wanted to play a creepy roguelike, and what I got was [i] so much more. [/i]

[h2] What is NO-SKIN? [/h2]

NO-SKIN is as such: take your typical turn-based roguelike, put in a non-linear story, add a dash of cosmic horror to  enhance the narrative elements, and make the turn-based combat [i] juuuuuust [/i] hard enough to make you think about what you need to do, and that's probably the best "on paper" description I can give this game. The game has a very pixelated style, but that does not stop it from often being gruesome and macabre (the name of the game is "NO-SKIN", what do you think it'll involve?). The narrative is at first sparse and confusing, but there are supplemental side stories you can unlock that flesh out each character in the game, which in turn builds the world around the basic story beats you began with and offer new perspectives. Staple on some appropriate atmospheric music and sounds, some unique enemy designs, and you have a neat little indie game in your hands.

That's NO-SKIN on the surface. Now, take whatever you have in mind and throw it out, because NO-SKIN will take your expectations and surprise you on how much it squeezes every drop out of each mechanic and element that is included in the package. Even if you're familiar with the subgenre, there is always more under the hood going on, or there's a new bit of information that makes you think "what if I tried that?" When it came to the next run, the next story I unlocked, the next character I unlocked, even the next event I hadn't seen yet, each hour I spent always seemed to have something new. It kept me guessing, it made me think, and it rewarded me for paying attention and gave me more of what I wanted. Even when I thought I knew what to expect, there was always something else, something more, and I went right back to digging.

I enjoyed it immensely, and that is because this is the kind of game that I love to play. Something that encourages my mind goblins and pushes me to explore everything that I possibly can, buy everything that I can, wade through the strange and unsettling themes and imagery, and try to think outside the box when I wasn't sure what to do next. If that is something that sounds interesting to you, then you and I are alike and you may get a good time out of this game.

[h2] This is a game for ME. But is it a game for YOU? [/h2]

I really, really want to gush about all that the game does that makes it so special, but this is truly a game that's worth going in as blind as can be. If what I've described and what is on the store page does not, at the least, make you curious, or you're not someone who likes roguelikes, potentially triggering themes [spoiler] (such as self harm, suicide, abuse, etc) [/spoiler] or games that will demand multiple successful runs to get everything out of it, then I can understand if that is a turn off for you. I got a lot out of this game both because I loved it and because it demanded as such. This is also a game that will very much demand you take screenshots or keep notes, because a lot of information and secrets need to be kept in mind for future playthroughs (especially if you want to understand what the actual fuck is going on in this game). You CAN just look up a guide and circumvent that, but a lot of the fun for me was putting that effort in to learn and piece together everything on my own, and I highly encourage that you do so as well.

This game is also, again, difficult when you first start, and successful runs unlock higher difficulties with specific modifiers that can also change how you approach things and make you strain your knowledge and resources to the brink. My tolerance is high for difficult games (I am very willing to bash my head in the wall until I hit the perfect run), so if yours isn't, understand that you can still do a lot, if not, most things if you aren't looking to unlock the next hardest difficulty. And if you want a story that's straightforward, well, this is not that kind of game. I have a good idea on the story of the game and what's up with certain parts (especially after the 1.2 update, thank you NoEye-Soft), but that is because I took the time to explore everything and take notes on what anyone said that seemed important. NO-SKIN is one of those rare horror games that refuses to tell you what it is right away, inviting curiosity instead of overwhelming players with exposition. Developed and published by NoEye-Soft, it presents itself as a roguelike with survival and mystery elements, but the first moments make it clear that it is also something stranger and more experimental. The premise is minimal, almost intentionally obscure—you awaken in a place that feels familiar yet wrong, and every hallway, room, and object seems to hint at a story hidden beneath the surface. Instead of relying on scripted cinematic horror, the game builds tension through ambiguity, atmosphere, and the unsettling awareness that you never fully understand what is happening. It is horror by implication rather than explanation, and that artistic restraint becomes one of its defining strengths.

The gameplay structure follows the familiar rhythm of roguelikes—enter a run, gather resources, survive encounters, uncover clues, retreat or die, and try again—but where other games emphasize progression and efficiency, NO-SKIN prioritizes discovery. Each attempt reveals new environmental details, character fragments, cryptic messages, and mechanical wrinkles that slowly reshape your understanding of the world. The procedural generation ensures that no two runs feel identical, but the sense of creeping dread persists regardless of layout. Inventory management, item decisions, and route planning matter, not because the systems are complicated, but because every choice feels like it could affect your survival or unlock new knowledge. The game trusts players to take notes, form theories, and draw conclusions rather than spoon-feeding answers.

One of the most distinctive aspects of NO-SKIN is its visual style—a stark blend of photographed textures, gritty realism, and pixel-rendered characters that appear slightly disconnected from their environments. This contrast makes the world feel uncanny, like a dream state where elements do not fully belong together. The lighting, shadows, and color palette lean into discomfort rather than spectacle, creating an uneasy liminality that lingers even in quiet moments. The sound design deepens the tension further: distant reverberations, muffled footsteps, static hums, and sparse musical cues give the impression that something is always present—just beyond the edge of perception. The horror comes not from what leaps out at you, but from what you imagine might be waiting.

Despite its mechanical simplicity, the game balances difficulty, unpredictability, and fairness in a way that encourages repeated attempts. Failure never feels like a dead end, because each death hints at new possibilities—missed rooms, untested pathways, forgotten items, or hidden interactions. Unlocks and carryover elements reward perseverance, offering subtle advantages or new tools that reshape later runs. The pacing remains tight, with little downtime or filler, and the best moments arise organically from unexpected situations rather than scripted scares. The game’s central antagonist, referenced in fragments as the “No-Skin Man,” serves less as a monster and more as a symbolic threat—something that represents the faceless, unknown terror behind the world’s fragmented narrative.

The narrative is another element left deliberately incomplete. Instead of providing a clearly defined plot, the game presents scattered clues—diary entries, object descriptions, environmental storytelling, and surreal imagery—that encourage speculation. Some players will piece together a cohesive interpretation, while others may embrace the uncertainty as part of the experience. This ambiguity will not appeal to everyone. Those who prefer explicit storytelling, clear-cut lore, or traditional progression may find the cryptic nature frustrating. Similarly, players accustomed to combat-heavy horror titles may feel the slower pace and interpretive design lack immediate payoff. But for players who enjoy discovering meaning rather than being handed it, the ambiguity becomes one of the game’s greatest draws.

As an indie project, NO-SKIN also benefits from its tightly focused vision. It doesn’t try to imitate bigger horror franchises or chase trends. Its systems are compact, its mechanics purposeful, and its presentation confidently unique. The replayability is strong not because of collectible checklists or sprawling content, but because the world remains intriguing long after the first few runs. The relatively low price, strong optimization, and positive community reception reinforce the sense that this is a passion-driven game built to surprise rather than simply entertain. It may not be tailored for every type of player, but it excels at what it sets out to do.

Ultimately, NO-SKIN succeeds because it trusts the player—trusts them to explore, to interpret, to persevere, and to feel discomfort without constant explanation. It offers a horror experience defined not by jump scares or violence, but by curiosity, atmosphere, and psychological tension. It is memorable, not because it overwhelms, but because it leaves enough unsaid for the imagination to fill the gaps. For players who appreciate experimental horror, roguelike uncertainty, and games that linger in the mind long after the screen goes dark, NO-SKIN is a compelling and unsettling journey worth taking.

Survive eldritch horrors, get stronger and deliver the No-Skin Man his skin before he runs out of patience and hunts you down- how hard could that be, right? Well, turns out things get a whole lot more... complicated. 

The basic gameplay loop is pretty straightforward- pick a playable character with some very weaksauce stats and a melee/ranged weapon of some sort, get dropped into a long gauntlet of rooms each with percentage odds of certain events or battles occurring, and try to survive as the No-Skin Man's doomsday timer ticks up to 100 after every event. However, you're always given a choice between which one of three rooms to explore next, and you get to see the possible outcomes of each room in advance. Strategically picking specific rooms and accumulating resources through battle and from merchants is a key part of keeping up with the increasingly difficult enemies you encounter.

The additional playable characters you can unlock have unique mechanics that make them noticeably more complex than the one you start off with, and some of the most satisfying gameplay moments to me in my playthrough was finally figuring out exactly how one of these characters ticked and how I needed to plan my items/events to deal with their individual challenges and unique events. You can end up feeling like an unstoppable demigod by the end of one of these runs but actually getting there, especially on the higher Faith difficulties, requires some careful resource management that adds some much needed difficulty to the game. 

And well- even if you manage to get to the end of a run, you'll find out very quickly that [i]reaching[/i] the No-Skin Man by no means ensures that you'll actually [i]have[/i] the skin you're supposed to be giving him in the first place. Figuring out how to beat the game for real- and how to get that singular achievement (which only has about 2.5% of players having earned it as of posting this review)- means unraveling the dark, unhinged lore of the game and its characters over multiple playthroughs, unlockable memory sessions and various in-game dialogue trees and puzzles. I don't want to spoil too much of what you'll experience as you dig deeper into the mountain of hidden content, other than to say that I would not be surprised if Yume Nikki and Omori were very big influences on the developer. Actually making the leap of logic needed to finally earn that achievement isn't all [i]that[/i] difficult but the game does make you feel pretty clever about it by the end of it all and even after all that there's still quite a lot of content left to explore. 

Overall No-Skin was a huge surprise to me for how much I enjoyed it and I'd recommend it to anyone who likes roguelikes and psychological horror RPGs in general.

[h1]A Simple And Effective "Tech Showcase"[/h1]

[h1]Things I Like About No Skin:[/h1]

[b]Some Compliments[/b]
[list]
[*]It's a turn-based roguelike with a focus on hoarding items and resource management. You need to choose which randomized encounter benefits you most and which you can take on with little hassle.
[*]Your power comes from the consumables you collect during the run. Unlike other actions(except Talk and Trade), using a consumable doesn't end you turn, so you can buff or heal yourself as much as you like. Buffs, however, only last for the current fight. It is wise not to over-buff and save some consumables for later more problematic encounters.
[*]And that's pretty much it. The game doesn't have some really crazy synergies to build around. All you need to do is hoard the right amount of consumables, use them moderately, sometimes pray for RNGeus for decent encounter generation, and you are good to go.
[*]The dev certainly nails the atmosphere. The simple MS Paint style works surprisingly well with the weird cast. Backgrounds may be static images but the distorted effect really amplifies the dream-like sequences. It's feels eerie and slightly intriguing.
[*]I like the idea of talking to certain characters can reveal a lot of information for future reference. Some enemies may give you more consumables should you be bring them certain items; some may even join you if you know how and when to talk to them.
[*]There's also a secondary game mode called Dream Diary. This mode serves more of a test ground for ideas or alternative mechanics that don't make it into the main game. It's refreshing to play around and you can unlock new upgrades for the main game mode if you complete them.
[*]Works Great With Steam Deck!
[/list]

[h1]Things I Dislike About No Skin:[/h1]

[b]Some Complaints[/b]
[list]
[*]The story is almost non-existent. It's a classic "keep it cryptic for cryptic sake". All the lore pieces feel inconsequential. The dialogues may shed some lights on the over-arching plotline but they ultimately fail to convey anything meaningful.
[*]Item menu could use some rework, adding more columns instead of scrolling down one single-file line.
[*]Because of the simplistic nature, repeated runs can easily become tedious.
[/list]

This game has been something of a comfort game for me during a really hard period in my life, so I may be biased in its favor. Just thought I should put that out there. 

That said, I've found it compelling and addictive. It's satisfying as a roguelike, especially if you're the sort of person (like me) who looks for the best way to exploit and break the game--a certain secret specifically relies on doing that. The gameplay serves as the backdrop for a complicated interpersonal drama that you unravel piece by piece, which I'm still not totally sure I 100% understand, but I know I haven't seen all the content in the game yet, either. The themes are very grim and gritty, which is very much to my taste. In order to unlock some things, there is a separate game mode that is much more of a puzzle game than a roguelike, and it tickles the part of my brain that loves to try to "solve" combat like a puzzle in the base game. It also turns your expectations on their head and each of the memory segments has impressed me in some way. The music is soft and moody and enhances the gameplay.

The biggest draw in this game, imo, is the secret-hunting. There's always something more to unravel, and it's good about giving you just the right amount of guidance to find something new. Every time I think I've got this game all figured out, it teases me with the next discovery.

It is going to require some patience, but if you typically like roguelikes, this should not be difficult for you. Most of the progression comes in the form of learning the game's ins and outs, rather than unlocking straight mechanical upgrades; you mostly unlock new opportunities for the chance for something good in future runs. 

I'd recommend this game. Maybe not to everybody, but definitely if you like roguelikes and psychological dread and very dark themes. This game's got heart. And blood.

No-Skin is both a maddeningly frustrating and INCREDIBLY satisfying game that is just as much brain-teaser puzzle as it is roguelike RPG. The story, at first, feels bare bones and poorly explained, but the deeper you delve into the plot, the more you uncover, until you find a magnificent story underneath. It won't simply offer the plot up on a silver platter, though. You will need to go looking to understand character motivations, and the driving force behind the roguelike gameplay loop. The turn-based battle system is snappy and fun while remaining challenging throughout, and the way it forces you to really think outside the box at multiple points in the story is both incredibly complex, and yet infuriatingly simple once you do find an intended solution. The game does not pull its punches when it comes to making you work to unlock new things, but it makes up for this effort by having a near non-stop wealth of secrets to unlock and find. Every time I think I've seen everything there is to see, No-Skin manages to pull out an entirely new facet to enjoy. Be warned, the guides and player supports online for this game are scarce, so you'll likely need to keep notes, be thorough, and really use your brain for some of the adversities the gameplay presents, but ultimately, No-Skin is a very rewarding experience, and I've greatly enjoyed picking it apart. If there's any single complaint I could make, it is only that I wish I hadn't stumbled upon the endgame solution so soon, so that I could continue to puzzle it out and enjoy it even longer. Even so, I will likely be returning to this game regularly for the foreseeable future, because even after beating and unlocking pretty much everything, to my knowledge, the gameplay loop is still incredibly fun, and I greatly enjoy trying different builds on different characters.

A few months ago, I reviewed Mouthwashing, and called it a sentimental experience. I'll be honest and say that I didn't fully understand the exact depths of the plot until reading the the debates going on about Jimmy. 

Why is that relevant to this? Because NO-SKIN feels like a game that's just as accusatory, yet in a slightly more whimsical way. It's gruesome, horrific and mystifying, the juxtaposition between edgy teenage dynamics in friend groups and Lovecraftian entities plaguing humanity and making you ask a question which should be so simple, yet has so many layers to it: What's real, and what's important?

Noire goes through her journey as a champion of the moon, which, in some respects, sounds more like... Uh, Sailor Moon, or any 90s/00s teen supernatural drama, but in reality, there's a lot of nuance to the journey. For a small, independent journey (both on the part of the player's run through the game, and the developer's creation of the game itself, the game feels huge. There's  hours upon hours of content, and the RNG beats the shit out of you at any opportunity as you attempt to carve and shoot your way through battle after battle with corrupted variants of your friends, cultists, monsters, otherworldly/interdimensional forces and even Gods. 

Every choice you make can put you in a fight, can help you find items, can help you buy items and upgrades, can increase the difficulty or decrease it - everything has its price. What are you willing to do to go further in the game? 
Complemented by the fact that there's also a currency that can be accumulated and used either at the start of each new run or in special circumstances, you're never shy of new things to discover.

The art isn't spectacular, but it doesn't have to be because much like Undertale, the Obra-Dynn, Blasphemous, and many other independent games, it still gets it's point across using a unique art style that captures the tone of the game. A beguiling, albeit cruel tone that's encapsulated in every fight where you get the ability to talk to your friends as they slowly mutate into bleak constructs of some of their most defining negative traits: Are you *really* a good person? 

It feels like one of those nightmares where the protagonist's closest allies are accusing them of toxic traits, and while you know the protagonist never meant to depict themselves that way, you're left wondering afterwards if maybe, just maybe, they had a point. 

I'll admit I haven't 100%'ed the game so take everything I've said with a grain of salt, but I think that's the beauty of art - I've completed the main task, but there's still so much left to discover, I still have memories left to acquire, and I'll still give this game a glowing review simply due to the fact that it is ruthlessly addictive.

NO-SKIN reminds me a little of Earthbound; it's not for everyone, it's pretty meta, it covers a lot of topics that might be challenging to take in, it's a little over the top, but something about this game also just feels very personal, and it feels like a love letter to a lot of the things that the developer has experienced. I like that. 9/10.

NO-SKIN is an incredible horror-rougelite that I couldn't put down. The game play itself is heavily RNG based where you choose to go into rooms with a set chance of something occurring. Given the nature of RNG, this can come off as frustrating, and I definitely had several instances where a run was doomed because I couldn't get the dice roll to meet the crimson dancers. However, I found that the RNG more often worked in your favor and serves as a means to differentiate each run. To combat the RNG, there are a number of encounters in the game that reward you for finding secrets and learning about the games systems. This was my favorite part of the game, the fact that I was rewarded for experimenting and finding optimal routes through different encounters. 

The story itself is also very interesting as it is never directly told to you. Much of it is left to the players interpretation regarding the different characters relationships and the overall story. You are given hints and clues through small conversations and played out scenes, but the rest is left for you to put together. I thought the way that it was delivered was very clever, although I could see an argument being made saying that it is lackluster. 

Overall, I really enjoyed my time with NO-SKIN. I think it is a great game that fans of abstract horror should give a try. There are some rough edges, such as repeating dialogue and some general ambiguity, but for this being a full title by a solo dev, there is a lot of great content that is genuinely impressive. I look forward to seeing what comes next from NoEye-Soft!

[h2] NO-SKIN Review – A Disturbingly Good Time [/h2]

Alright, so I went into NO-SKIN not knowing exactly what to expect, but I came out fully hooked. This game is weird, unsettling, and seriously addictive. It’s got that perfect mix of roguelike randomness and psychological horror that keeps you on edge the entire time.

[h3] Gameplay & Mechanics [/h3] 
You’re thrown into this eerie, almost dreamlike house with rooms that shift every run, forcing you to think on your feet. There’s turn-based combat, resource management, and a constant sense of dread as you try to survive encounters with the No-Skin Man. Every playthrough feels different, which keeps things fresh even when you inevitably die and restart. The strategy side of it is solid—every move matters, and wasting resources can get you killed fast.

I like that it doesn’t hold your hand. You figure things out as you go, and that slow unraveling of how things work is part of what makes it so engaging. It reminds me of games like Fear and Hunger or World of Horror, where the tension comes from both the gameplay and the disturbing atmosphere.

[h3] Atmosphere & Aesthetics [/h3] 
The art style is something else. It’s a mix of pixel art characters and realistic, almost photographic backgrounds, which gives the whole game an uncanny, off-putting feel. Like, you know something is wrong just by looking at it. The soundtrack and ambient noises? Creepy as hell. The kind that makes you hesitate before going into the next room.

There were moments where I just sat there, debating whether I really wanted to keep moving forward—not because I was bored, but because the game does such a good job of getting under your skin. The horror here isn’t about jumpscares; it’s about slowly realizing how messed up everything around you is.

[h3] Story & Lore [/h3] 
The story is vague at first, but the more you play, the more you start piecing things together. Clues are hidden everywhere, and there’s a real sense of discovery each time you unlock a new "memory" or find some cryptic note that changes how you see things.

I won’t spoil anything, but if you’re the kind of person who loves digging into lore and unraveling mysteries, this game delivers. It’s one of those experiences where the more you learn, the more unsettling it all gets.

[h3] Final Thoughts [/h3] 
NO-SKIN is easily one of the best indie horror roguelikes I’ve played in a while. It’s tough, it’s creepy, and it keeps you coming back for more. The gameplay is strategic without being frustrating, the atmosphere is genuinely unnerving, and the story is just cryptic enough to keep you engaged without feeling aimless. Reminds me of Fear & Hunger.

If you’re into roguelikes with a strong horror vibe, this is absolutely worth checking out. I’ll definitely be diving back in to see what else I can uncover.

[h2] Final Score: 9/10 – Messed up in the best way possible. [/h2]

[h3]Skin DLC when?[/h3]
[b]No-Skin[/b] is what happens when a horror game doesn’t [i]forget[/i] the monsters—it just makes them look like guilt, anxiety, or your ex in a skin sack.

It’s [b]turn-based, lo-fi, and socially threatening[/b]. You move through cursed rooms like a bad dream you can’t stop apologizing for. Every turn is a choice: stab, run, ask someone a weird question. Then deal with the consequences, usually bleeding.

[b]Combat[/b] is tactical in the worst way. Not complicated... [i]cruel[/i]. You make decisions with information(?) and bad odds. You have a knife. Maybe a gun. The rest is [i]situational dread management[/i].

There are no spells. No skill trees. Just desperation, momentum, and whatever luck you didn’t spend last run. You’re not building a character... you’re [b]burning one down[/b].

[b]The house loops.[/b] The art looks like a haunted zine drawn during a fever nap. The tone cuts like budget Silent Hill filtered through breakup texts and brain fog.

[B]Stare too long and it stares back. Bleeds weird. Good game.[/b]

Very unique atmosphere and setting,I dig the simplistic pixel graphics a lot. The raw combat loop is good and the sound effects add a lot to it but the runs themselves aren't very varied in terms of traditional builds in contrast to it's nature. Basically,every decision you make in the game is RNG. Whether it's the rooms,the encounters inside the rooms,the accuracy of your weapons and even the accuracy of some of the items in your inventory. That being said,the encounters themselves have fixed loot tables,so you always know what to expect from an enemy after killing it once. The shops themselves also have fixed items,though they change depending on your progression in the run. Notice I've said that weapon accuracy is also RNG related,so sometimes losing a run is completely out of your control. That being said,the recruit mechanic is pretty fun and adds a little more depth to the decision making and the combat encounters.
Moving onto the story,it's quite literally all over the place. In addition to permanent upgrades you get after finishing a run,you also get some information about the characters and the setting of the world,though it isn't really explained clearly and requires you to piece a lot of things to get a full grasp. This wouldn't be a bad thing if the game wasn't so incredibly vague about what it's trying to tell. I didn't fully finish the story yet though,so my opinion on this section may change. 
My biggest pet peeve so far is how the game keeps retelling you the major mechanics/story bits over and over regardless of if you've seen them. For example,if an enemy inflicts a status effect on you,the game tells you what it is and how to get rid of it. For the first time it's obviously fine,but it keeps saying it on every new run,it also plays out the entire cutscene after finishing a run over and over,with no way to fully skip it easily.
I deliberately didn't get into the spoilers as they are the best sections the game has to offer IMO and I'd fully recommend the players to experience it blindly,some of the content there majorly removes the RNG aspect and displays very interesting information about the characters you play or fight against.
All that aside though,it is a good game. None of my complaints are really major deal breakers for such a distinct experience made by one person and I want to see more projects like this.
On a final note,big shoutout to the dev for recovering my save file. The game doesn't have a cloud system so you have to manually backup the files,you can directly reach out to him should you fail to do remember. He's making a new game of similiar nature as of now and I'd recommend you check that out as well. Best wishes.

Edit: After putting more hours into this game, this is one of the most criminally underrated horror games I've ever played. As a turn-based tactics roguelike the gameplay isn't anything new, but the atmosphere, the soundtrack, the overall vibe is so good, and it conceals so many secrets. There are so many ways it could have gone wrong: it could have come off juvenile or trying too hard to be edgy, its contrast between the characters being teenagers dealing with teenage insecurities and the more cosmic horror underlying that could have been weak, but it somehow manages to maintain a sense of horrific gravitas amidst everything. I could not more strongly recommend this game.

Not Horror, Not Roguelike—Just a Repetitive Grind

    Shallow Gameplay & Lack of Depth
        The game lacks any meaningful mechanics, relying instead on vague imagery of dark spaces to pass as a horror game.
        There’s no real tension or fear factor—just a loop of repetitive scenes.

    Repetitive & Unrewarding Roguelike Elements
        Events are highly repetitive, often appearing multiple times in a single run.
        Rooms can be re-entered with the same events occurring, killing any sense of unpredictability.
        Unlocking new rooms is tied to how much you play, but it feels like a forced grind rather than organic progression.

    Fragmented Scene-Based Design
        Every event and room is a separate scene you swap between, which becomes visually tiring over time.
        There’s no immersive flow—just a collection of disconnected moments stitched together.

    Confusing & Unclear Mechanics
        Gun mechanics feel broken—an 85% accuracy gun missing five shots in a row, while a knife is somehow more reliable.
        The UI is a disaster:
            Essential item details require extra steps to check.
            Inventory is cluttered, with the bag awkwardly placed in the middle of everything.

    Artificial & Forced Progression
        Instead of natural discovery, progression feels locked behind arbitrary playtime gates.
        The core loop is going through the same rooms, seeing the same events, which makes no sense in a horror setting.

    Illogical Design Choices
        The game uses a shower as a healing mechanic, which feels ridiculous in a haunted house filled with murderous entities.
        Alternative healing options like a medical cabinet, a moment of respite, or even vomiting due to the house’s atmosphere would make far more thematic sense.

Final Thoughts

The game has potential, but it desperately needs improvements. The devs should focus on:
✅ Reducing repetition and increasing event variety.
✅ Making progression feel rewarding rather than locked behind grind mechanics.
✅ Clarifying mechanics and improving the UI.
✅ Reworking immersion-breaking elements like the bizarre healing system.

Until then, this game fails both as a horror experience and as a roguelike. Not recommended.

It's a confident game with good art and many nooks to it. I have two problems though. 

1) It's not a roguelike, like it says in the description. All content is present every run -- like how the merchant frogs (the moon goddess have mercy on their souls) always have a set item list. The rooms all have the same loot. You can farm the non-random events. So you can choose your playstyle out in advance, and not have to react to randomness. It's like a puzzler RPG with permadeath -- which is fine in itself, but I feel a bit misled. 

2) The game has some UI problems that slow you down. The game explains status effects EVERY TIME, requiring you to hit a button to advance. It's the same for talking and trading. Read the flavor text of the long-gilled fish? Get ready to skip past four text screens each time you want to buy something. For a game that is meant to be replayed and replayed, this really became tedious and made me not want to continue. Probably 1/2 my play time (literally) was pressing Z (odd default bindings) to advance.
